The [conjugate-prior page](conjugate-priors.qmd#collecting-powers) updated a beta prior after observing the Turkish UniMorph sample. We now ask what the exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model predicted before those rows were observed.

The calculation uses [conditional probability](../foundations/conditional-probability.qmd) to specify a count distribution at each parameter value and then [expectation](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd) to average those conditional probabilities over the prior. The future indicators are conditionally [independent](../foundations/independence.qmd) given the shared parameter; their unconditional dependence contributes to the predictive [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd).

The calculation asks us to average the conditional binomial count probability over possible values of its shared parameter. We will perform that integral, reproduce the resulting beta-binomial distribution by simulation, and then compare the superpopulation prediction with the actual without-replacement design used to select the analyzed UniMorph rows.

## From a parameter prior to possible counts

Under the counterfactual exchangeable-superpopulation design,

$$
\Theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),
$$

and, conditional on $\Theta=\theta$, a block count satisfies

$$
\widetilde K\mid\Theta=\theta
\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(m,\theta).
$$

The [**prior predictive distribution**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introBDA.html) averages the binomial mass over the prior density:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde K=r)
&=
\int_0^1
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde K=r\mid\Theta=\theta)
f_\Theta(\theta)\,\mathrm d\theta\\
&=
\int_0^1
\binom mr\theta^r(1-\theta)^{m-r}
\frac{\theta^{\alpha-1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}}
{B(\alpha,\beta)}
\,\mathrm d\theta\\
&=
\frac{\binom mr}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
\int_0^1
\theta^{r+\alpha-1}
(1-\theta)^{m-r+\beta-1}
\,\mathrm d\theta\\
&=
\binom mr
\frac{B(r+\alpha,m-r+\beta)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The last integral is the definition of the beta function. This derivation shows why the beta-binomial is not an unrelated new family: it is the binomial sampling mass averaged over beta-distributed uncertainty about one block-level probability.

This is the beta-binomial mass function. It makes parameter uncertainty visible in the units that the design records: the number of *t*-initial cells in a block of lexeme--paradigm rows.

```{r}
#| label: load-unimorph-prior-predictive
library(ggplot2)

sample_120 <- read.csv(
  "data/unimorph-turkish/verb-past-sample-120.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
m <- nrow(sample_120)
observed_k <- sum(sample_120$t_initial)
unit_count <- 1L
alpha <- unit_count
beta <- unit_count
support <- 0:m

prior_mass <- exp(
  lchoose(m, support) +
    lbeta(support + alpha, m - support + beta) -
    lbeta(alpha, beta)
)
prior_predictive <- data.frame(count = support, probability = prior_mass)

prior_mean <- m * alpha / (alpha + beta)
prior_variance <- m * alpha * beta * (alpha + beta + m) /
  ((alpha + beta)^2 * (alpha + beta + 1))

stopifnot(
  m == 120L, observed_k == 42L,
  abs(sum(prior_predictive$probability) - 1) < 1e-12
)
data.frame(m, observed_k, prior_mean, prior_variance)
```

With the $\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)$ prior and observed block size `r m`, the prior predictive expectation and variance are

$$
\mathbb{E}[\widetilde K]
=m\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\widetilde K]
=
m\frac{\alpha\beta}{(\alpha+\beta)^2}
\frac{\alpha+\beta+m}{\alpha+\beta+1}.
$$

They evaluate to `r sprintf("%.3f", prior_mean)` and `r sprintf("%.3f", prior_variance)`. The variance is large because one $\theta$ is drawn for the complete block, then all cells in that block share it.

With $\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)$, the model assigns the same prior predictive mass to every count from zero through $m$. Extreme and central block counts consequently receive equal probability before the data. The plot makes this broad predictive commitment available for criticism.

```{r}
#| label: plot-unimorph-prior-predictive
#| fig-cap: "Exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation prior predictive mass for a 120-cell independent block. The line marks the count in the observed 120-row sample."
ggplot(prior_predictive, aes(count, probability)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey35", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed_k, color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "t-initial forms in 120 lexeme cells", y = "Prior-predictive probability") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Generating the same distribution

The integral can also be simulated in the order specified by the model: draw one $\theta^{(s)}$ for a block, then draw its count.

```{r}
#| label: simulate-unimorph-prior-predictive
set.seed(2026101801)
simulation_count <- 40000L
theta_prior <- rbeta(simulation_count, alpha, beta)
k_prior <- rbinom(simulation_count, size = m, prob = theta_prior)

stopifnot(abs(mean(k_prior) - prior_mean) < .5)
c(simulated_mean = mean(k_prior), analytic_mean = prior_mean,
  simulated_variance = var(k_prior), analytic_variance = prior_variance)
```

Drawing a fresh $\theta$ before every cell would define a different model. It would average the Bernoulli probability cell by cell and lose the block-level variation represented by the beta-binomial distribution.

In fact, if every cell received an independent $\Theta_i\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$, then each marginal success probability would be $\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)$ and the block count would be binomial with that fixed probability. Sharing one $\Theta$ induces positive dependence among cells after $\Theta$ is averaged out.

## The finite-population restriction

The prior predictive distribution follows a counterfactual operation: draw one shared probability from the beta prior, then draw an independent Bernoulli block. The actual sample of 120 UniMorph rows was selected without replacement from a known finite table, which gives a hypergeometric randomization distribution. And because UniMorph records lexical types without usage counts, neither calculation describes token frequency in Turkish use.

Prior prediction remains useful here because it makes that model's commitment explicit. The [posterior predictive page](predictive-distributions.qmd) will put the independent-draw prediction beside the corresponding finite-population prediction.

## Recap and forward link

1. A prior predictive distribution averages possible observations over the parameter prior.
2. The beta-binomial follows by recognizing a beta-function integral.
3. One shared $\Theta$ per block induces extra count variation; one fresh $\Theta_i$ per cell defines a different model.
4. Prior-predictive breadth is a model commitment that should be checked on the observed-count scale.

The [posterior predictive page](predictive-distributions.qmd#prediction-under-the-exchangeable-bernoulli-model) repeats the averaging after the sample updates the prior.

## Check your understanding

1. Why is the predictive outcome a count rather than a value of $\Theta$?
2. Why must one simulated block use one shared draw of $\theta$?
3. Which part of the variance reflects uncertainty about $\Theta$?
4. Why is this beta-binomial mass not the sample's actual randomization distribution?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The prediction concerns what the design records in a future block: the number of *t*-initial lexeme cells, after averaging over uncertainty in $\Theta$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Draw one $\theta$ for the block, then draw all cells conditionally independently given that $\theta$. Averaging over the shared $\theta$ induces the positive dependence and extra beta-binomial variation. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The beta-binomial overdispersion factor, equivalently the variation in the conditional mean $m\Theta$, reflects uncertainty about $\Theta$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The actual 120 rows were sampled without replacement from a known 588-row resource, so their randomization distribution is hypergeometric rather than beta-binomial. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
